question: How often does REALM rebuild its document index while the retriever is being trained?
reference_answer: Every several hundred training steps: all documents are asynchronously re-embedded and re-indexed, so the index is slightly stale between refreshes.

evidence.quote: asynchronously re-embedding and re-indexing all documents every several hundred training steps

question: When monoBERT scores a query against a passage, how long can the query be before it gets cut off?
reference_answer: The query is truncated to at most 64 tokens.

evidence.quote: We truncate the query to have at most 64 tokens.

question: Why does adding more retrieved passages not make the Fusion-in-Decoder encoder's cost explode?
reference_answer: Each passage is encoded independently, so self-attention only runs over one passage at a time; computation grows linearly with the number of passages instead of quadratically. The passages are only combined in the decoder.

evidence.quote: Processing passages independently in the encoder allows to scale to large number of contexts, as it only performs self attention over one context at a time.

question: What is the difference between the two RAG model variants in how they use retrieved documents while generating?
reference_answer: RAG-Sequence uses the same retrieved document to generate the whole output, while RAG-Token can rely on a different retrieved document for each generated token.

evidence.quote: The RAG-Sequence model uses the same retrieved document to generate the complete sequence.
In the RAG-Token model we can draw a different latent document for each target token and marginalize accordingly.

question: In the multi-document QA experiments, how badly can GPT-3.5-Turbo do with 20 or 30 documents when the answer is in the middle, compared with answering from memory alone?
reference_answer: In the worst case it does worse than the closed-book setting with no documents at all (56.1%); performance can drop by more than 20% when the relevant document is in the middle.

evidence.quote: performance in 20- and 30-document settings is lower than performance without any input documents

notes: Source: 2.3 Results and Discussion. Closed-book baseline is 56.1%.

question: When DPR is trained with in-batch negatives, does it keep helping to add more hard negatives found by keyword search?
reference_answer: No. Adding one BM25 hard negative per batch improves results substantially, but adding a second one does not help further.

evidence.quote: We find that adding a single BM25 negative passage improves the result substantially while adding two does not help further.

notes: Source: 5.2 Ablation Study on Model Training > In-batch negative training.

question: How do RAG and Fusion-in-Decoder differ in the way they combine information from several retrieved passages?
reference_answer: RAG treats the retrieved document as a latent variable and marginalizes the generator's predictions over the retrieved documents. Fusion-in-Decoder encodes each passage separately and fuses the evidence only in the decoder, which attends over all encoded passages together.

evidence.quote: To train the retriever and generator end-to-end, we treat the retrieved document as a latent variable.
The model thus performs evidence fusion in the decoder only, and we refer to it as Fusion-in-Decoder.

notes: Sources: RAG 2 Methods; FiD 3 Method > Reading.

question: DPR reports a large win over BM25 on open-domain QA. Does that advantage hold when DPR is tested zero-shot across the BEIR datasets?
reference_answer: No. In its own paper DPR clearly beats BM25 (65.2% vs. 42.9% top-5 accuracy on Natural Questions), but in BEIR's zero-shot evaluation DPR generalizes worst of all the evaluated models, while BM25 remains a strong baseline.

evidence.quote: It not only outperforms BM25 by a large margin (65.2% vs. 42.9% in Top-5 accuracy)
DPR, the only non-MSMARCO trained dataset overall performs the worst in generalization on the benchmark.

notes: Sources: DPR 1 Introduction; BEIR 5 Results and Analysis (finding 3).

question: How big is the collection RAG retrieves from, compared with the database RETRO searches at evaluation time?
reference_answer: RAG retrieves from Wikipedia split into disjoint 100-word chunks, about 21M documents. RETRO's evaluation retrieval database contains 1.75T tokens (600B tokens during training).

evidence.quote: Each Wikipedia article is split into disjoint 100-word chunks, to make a total of 21M documents.
The evaluation retrieval database thus contains 1.75T tokens.

notes: Sources: RAG 3 Experiments; RETRO 2.1 Training dataset. RETRO's abstract and 2.3 round the database to '2 trillion tokens'; 2.1 gives the exact 1.75T (evaluation) and 600B (training).

question: How many dimensions does each of ColBERT's per-token vectors have?
reference_answer: 128 dimensions (and the number of query embeddings is fixed at 32).

evidence.quote: We set our ColBERT embedding dimension $m$ to be 128

notes: Source: 4.1.2 Implementation. BEIR's latency table (2104.08663, Table 3) also lists ColBERT at 128 dimensions.

question: Across BEIR's zero-shot datasets, how often does re-ranking BM25 results with a cross-encoder beat plain BM25, and where does it fall short?
reference_answer: It beats BM25 on 16 of the 18 datasets, the best of all evaluated systems. It only fails on ArguAna and Touché-2020, two tasks that are very different from its MS MARCO training data.

evidence.quote: The cross-attentional re-ranking model (BM25+CE) performs the best and is able to outperform BM25 on almost all (16/18) datasets.
It only fails on ArguAna and Touché-2020, two retrieval tasks that are extremely different to the MS MARCO training dataset.

question: During training, how does RETRO avoid having to look up similar chunks live at every step?
reference_answer: Live retrieval would be too slow for training, so because the BERT embedder is frozen, RETRO precomputes the approximate nearest neighbours for all the training data and stores them with the data.

evidence.quote: we leverage the frozen aspect of the embedding operator Bert to precompute all approximate nearest neighbours and save the results as part of the data

notes: Source: 2.3 Nearest neighbour retrieval > Retrieval neighbours.
